content: Stavudine, a nucleoside analogue of thymidine, undergoes phosphorylation by cellular kinases to form its active metabolite, stavudine triphosphate. This active metabolite inhibits HIV-1 reverse transcriptase by competing with the natural substrate, thymidine triphosphate, and by causing DNA chain termination after its incorporation into viral DNA. Additionally, stavudine triphosphate inhibits cellular DNA polymerases β and γ, significantly reducing mitochondrial DNA synthesis. The antiviral activity of stavudine has been evaluated in cell culture using peripheral blood mononuclear cells, monocytic cells, and lymphoblastoid cell lines. Its effective concentration (EC50) ranges from 0.009 to 4 µM against both laboratory and clinical isolates of HIV-1. In cell culture, stavudine demonstrated additive to antagonistic activity when combined with zidovudine. However, when combined with abacavir, didanosine, tenofovir, or zalcitabine, it exhibited additive to synergistic anti-HIV-1 activity. The relationship between cell culture susceptibility of HIV-1 to stavudine and its inhibition of HIV-1 replication in humans has not been established. HIV-1 isolates with reduced susceptibility to stavudine have been selected in cell culture and have also been identified in patients treated with stavudine. Phenotypic analysis of HIV-1 isolates from 61 patients receiving prolonged stavudine monotherapy (6–29 months) revealed that post-therapy isolates from four patients exhibited EC50 values more than 4-fold higher (ranging from 7to 16-fold) than the average pretreatment susceptibility of baseline isolates. Among these, isolates from one patient contained zidovudine-resistance-associated substitutions T215Y and K219E, while isolates from another patient contained the multiple-nucleoside-resistance-associated substitution Q151M. Mutations in the reverse transcriptase (RT) gene of HIV-1 isolates from the other two patients were not detected. The genetic basis for changes in stavudine susceptibility has not been identified. Cross-resistance among HIV-1 reverse transcriptase inhibitors has been observed. Prolonged stavudine treatment has been shown to select for and/or maintain thymidine analogue mutations (TAMs), including M41L, D67N, K70R, L210W, T215Y/F, and K219Q/E, which are associated with zidovudine resistance. HIV-1 isolates with one or more TAMs exhibit reduced susceptibility to stavudine in cell culture. These TAMs occur at a similar frequency with both stavudine and zidovudine in virological treatment. Clinically, these findings suggest that stavudine should be avoided in the presence of thymidine analogue mutations.
